routes.description: Establish Christian revelation as the necessary precondition for truth, logic, knowledge, induction, evidence, and reasonable belief in God.
routes.successCriteria: Show that the Christian God supplies the required foundation for intelligibility and that denying this foundation leaves the con account unable to justify its own reasoning.

motionBridge.description: Connect God's truth and necessary epistemic role to the conclusion that belief in the Christian God is reasonable.

centralBridges.description: Establish that objective truth and knowledge require conformity to an absolute divine mind.
Establish that logical absolutes reflect God's thinking and cannot be grounded by autonomous naturalistic cognition.
Establish divine revelation as a certainty-conferring source available to human knowers.
Establish that nonrevelatory attempts to justify induction depend circularly on induction itself.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish Christian revelation from competing religious authorities through internal consistency tests.
Clarify that Christianity functions as the argument's starting precondition rather than as an inference from generic absolutes.

routes.description: Defend fallibilist, evidence-responsive inquiry as sufficient for reasonable belief while requiring support for Christianity's claimed epistemic necessity.
routes.successCriteria: Show that reasonableness does not require absolute certainty, that logic and experience support provisional knowledge, and that revelation and Christian exclusivity require independent demonstration.

motionBridge.description: Connect justified fallibilist inquiry and unmet theistic evidential burdens to withholding belief in God as presently unreasonable.

centralBridges.description: Define reasonable belief by valid inference and supported premises rather than by absolute certainty.
Ground inquiry in logical absolutes, shared experience, and appropriately limited confidence without adding God.
Require demonstration that Christianity uniquely accounts for logic, truth, and knowledge rather than merely asserting it.
Require a reliable mechanism connecting purported divine revelation to accurate human knowledge.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend induction as probabilistic justification without recasting it as deductive certainty.
Use disagreement among religious claims to require a truth-tracking method for selecting among revelations.

sections.title: Reasonableness, truth, and the burden of belief
sections.rationale: This issue fixes the motion-level standard and determines whether truth itself establishes reasonable theistic belief or whether supported premises and valid inference remain necessary.

sections.title: Objective reality, certainty, and radical skepticism
sections.rationale: The competing accounts of access to reality determine whether uncertainty about ultimate reality defeats secular knowledge or permits inquiry from minimal fallibilist commitments.

sections.title: The foundation and intelligibility of logic
sections.rationale: Accounting for logical absolutes is a central burden because both routes rely on logic while disputing whether its intelligibility requires the Christian God.

sections.title: Revelation, reliability, and rival religious claims
sections.rationale: The reliability and distinctiveness of Christian revelation govern whether it can bridge divine omniscience to human certainty and distinguish Christianity from competing authorities.

sections.title: Induction and the direction of the transcendental argument
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether probabilistic prediction can be rational without revelation and clarifies whether Christianity is established from shared premises or installed as the necessary starting point.
